Use this page when a laboratory value is part of your study: an exposure,
a covariate at baseline or an outcome (for example HbA1c or creatinine). You
need your cohort from [Phase 10](build-study-population.qmd) and the list of
analysis codes you want. You end with an `.rds` file of results for your
cohort, one row per result, filtered to the cohort before `collect()`. The
column dictionary is [Laboratoriedatabasens
Forskertabel](register-reference.qmd#lab-forsker).

## What the laboratory table is: LAB_F, not DST, not LPR {#not-a-dst-register-and-not-lpr}

**LAB_F** (Laboratoriedatabasens Forskertabel) is delivered by
Sundhedsdatastyrelsen (SDS) through Forskerservice. In the clinical
epidemiology literature it is usually called **RLRR** (Register of Laboratory
Results for Research). It is not on DST's register list.

It is not LPR. LPR is hospital contacts. This table is one row per laboratory
result. It is very large, so `semi_join()` and
`filter()` have to run before `collect()`.

## One delivery, several table names {#one-delivery-several-names}

`lab_dm_forsker`, `lab_forsker` and `laboratorieproevesvar` are cuts of the
same delivery, not separate registers. Using more than one double-counts.
Column names are not the same in every cut.

The [dictionary section](register-reference.qmd#lab-forsker) names the columns
this extract uses on `lab_dm_forsker`: `patient_cpr`, `analysiscode`,
`samplingdate`, `value`, `unit`. The Version 4 dictionary has more columns
than that. A delivery may not include every column in the dictionary, so do
not treat a full dictionary listing as the column list of the file you were
sent.

- **`lab_dm_forsker`:** person column `patient_cpr`, result column `value`.
- **`lab_forsker`:** a narrower cut of the same delivery (fewer columns).
- **`laboratorieproevesvar`:** a narrow cut seen in at least one project
  delivery. The person column is `cprnummer` and the result column is
  `samplevalue`, not `patient_cpr` and `value`. The guide's schema describes
  this cut as four columns and names those two. It does not name the other
  two; check them with `colnames()` on your own file.

## The October 2025 delivery: table names may change {#the-october-2025-delivery-is-unresolved}

::: {.callout-warning}
**Sundhedsdatastyrelsen updated the laboratory delivery on 3 October 2025**
([announcement
→](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/data-og-registre/forskerservice/om-forskerservice/nyheder-fra-forskerservice/2025/data_laboratoriedatabasen_031025)):
"Det nye LAB erstatter den tidligere version af LAB" (the new LAB replaces
the earlier version of LAB). The announcement names
four tables, `laboratorieproevesvar`, `Dimlaboratoriekoder`, `DimNPU` and
`Proevesvar_optaelling`, but never mentions `lab_dm_forsker` by name, and does
not say what happens to projects already using it. The official data
dictionary the guide is built from
([PDF](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/Media/638651043236441510/Dokumentation%20af%20Labdatabasens%20Forskertabel.pdf))
is Version 4, dated 1 December 2023, nearly two years *before* that
announcement, and it documents `lab_dm_forsker` only. Whether
`lab_dm_forsker` is being retired, and what `laboratorieproevesvar`'s columns
are after the October 2025 change, we do not know. Check the order
sheet ("bestillingsark") on Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's site, or your own
delivery, before relying on either name.
:::

## Extract lab results for your cohort {#the-pattern}

You choose the analysis codes. Laboratory tests are coded in NPU
(Nomenclature for Properties and Units), a terminology maintained by IFCC and
IUPAC and used for laboratory results in Denmark, Norway and Sweden ([NPU
leaflet, IUPAC
2019](https://iupac.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/NPUterminologi2019_Leaflet.pdf)).
Look up the codes for your tests at
[npu-terminology.org](https://www.npu-terminology.org), and write the list
and its source into your code.

`read_register()` requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see
[Parquet and fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) if you
did not convert them from SAS yourself. The register name below is the
`lab_dm_forsker` cut. If your file is `laboratorieproevesvar`, rename
`cprnummer` to `pnr` and keep `samplevalue` instead of `value`.

```r
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(arrow) # open_dataset() - fallback without fastreg
library(dplyr)

cohort_pnrs <- unique(readRDS("path/to/full_cohort.rds")$pnr) # your cohort from Phase 10

# Your own list of codes: look them up, the guide gives none.
# NPU and DNK codes both sit in analysiscode. There is no column called npu.
npu_codes <- c("REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_CODE")

lab <- read_register("lab_dm_forsker") %>% # without fastreg: open_dataset("path/to/lab_dm_forsker/")
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  rename(pnr = patient_cpr) %>% # laboratorieproevesvar: rename(pnr = cprnummer)
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>% # ONLY your cohort
  filter(analysiscode %in% npu_codes) %>% # filter BEFORE collect
  select(pnr, analysiscode, samplingdate, value, unit) %>% # samplevalue, not value, on laboratorieproevesvar
  collect() # only HERE is data pulled into RAM

saveRDS(lab, "path/to/extract_laboratory.rds")
```

The table stays one row per result. Collapse to one row per person only when
your definition needs that, the same way as in [Long and wide
format](long-wide.qmd).

### Synthetic data, on your own computer

[`fiktive`](https://github.com/sara-schwartz/fiktive) can build a
`lab_dm_forsker` table for local practice. It is not on DST. This synthetic
table has not been run against a DST delivery, so do not treat it as a check
that the pipeline works on the server.

Install once with `remotes::install_github("sara-schwartz/fiktive")`, as in
[Phase 6](first-extraction.qmd#preparation-install-fiktive-and-generate-synthetic-data).
To use real IFCC/NPU terms, set `options(fiktive.labterm_fetch_ifcc = TRUE)`
before generating. That option downloads and caches a public IFCC code list.
`FIKTIVE_LABTERM` (or `options(fiktive.labterm)`) is the other route: a
LabTerm or IFCC file you already have, not a download. Without one of those,
`fiktive` does not invent NPU codes. Do not take column names from `fiktive`'s
`labka` generator. That is a different database (LABKA, see
[Coverage](#coverage)).

```r
# remotes::install_github("sara-schwartz/fiktive")
options(fiktive.labterm_fetch_ifcc = TRUE) # or set FIKTIVE_LABTERM to a file you have

library(fiktive) # synthetic register data, local only
library(dplyr)

schema <- load_registers_schema()
pop <- generate_background_population(n = 60, seed = 1, schema = schema)
tables <- generate_registers(
  registers = c("lab_dm_forsker"),
  population = pop,
  schema = schema,
  from = as.Date("2015-01-01"),
  to = as.Date("2020-12-31"),
  seed = 1
)

# Then the same rename, semi_join, filter, and select as above,
# on tables$lab_dm_forsker instead of read_register().
```

## Which results reach the table {#what-reaches-the-table}

NPU is not its own column. It sits inside `analysiscode`, together with DNK
codes: codes for local Danish use, kept in the same NPU database but marked
"DNK" instead of "NPU" ([NPU
database](https://npu-terminology.org/npu-database/)). Only those coded results
reach the table, about 95 per cent. A
laboratory's own local codes never arrive. There is nothing to filter them in
with.

Patients who declined consent are absent from the table. That absence is not a
coded value, so there is no code to filter on.

## Coverage: from 2008, complete per laboratory by 2010-2016 {#coverage}

Coverage starts in 2008, not the 1990s. Complete coverage arrives per
laboratory between 2010 and 2016. The start year, the table of periods per
region and laboratory, the 95 per cent and the consent rule above are all in
Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's [documentation of the research
table](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/Media/638651043236441510/Dokumentation%20af%20Labdatabasens%20Forskertabel.pdf).
See also [Laboratoriedatabasen
→](https://sundhedsdatastyrelsen.dk/data-og-registre/nationale-sundhedsregistre/laboratoriedatabasen).

For years before 2008, projects used the separate regional database LABKA
([Arendt et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S245060); [Grann et al.
2011](https://doi.org/10.2147/CLEP.S17901)). Neither paper gives literal
column names, so the guide gives none.

## Results are text: convert `value` with care {#value-is-text}

`value` is text, not a number. Alongside numeric results the reference
section lists `POSITIV`, `NEGATIV`, `IKKE PÅVIST`, `INGEN VÆKST` and the
blood-type codes. `as.numeric()` turns every one of them into `NA`. R prints only
"NAs introduced by coercion", which is easy to miss in a long script, and the
result is that exactly the samples where something was found are dropped. The
same would happen to any result written with a sign, such as `<5`. On `laboratorieproevesvar` the same column is called `samplevalue`.

Before you convert, list the values that are not plain numbers, and decide
what each should become:

```r
library(dplyr) # filter, count

lab %>%
  filter(is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value)))) %>% # everything as.numeric() would turn into NA
  count(analysiscode, value, sort = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**Do not compare a numeric result across laboratories, or across time, without
`unit`.** The same `analysiscode` can mean a different scale when the
equipment or the sample material differs, including inside one laboratory over
time. Keep `unit` in the extract.
:::
